name: AFC Wimbledon
label: Fans re-founded the club and brought it home
why: Supporters founded AFC Wimbledon in 2002 after Wimbledon FC was moved to Milton Keynes, climbed from the ninth tier to the EFL, and returned to Plough Lane in 2020 with a fan bond that raised over £5m rather than give up Dons Trust control. The Ownership score credits trust ownership, not the re-founding itself.

name: Exeter City
label: Supporters' Trust rescue and ownership
why: In 2003, after relegation and the arrest of club figures for financial irregularities, the Supporters' Trust took over the club and about £4.5m of debt, stabilised it through a CVA and volunteer work, and has owned it for 23 years.

name: Heart of Midlothian
label: Foundation of Hearts rescue and fan ownership
why: Supporter pledges through the Foundation of Hearts helped save the club from administration in 2013 and took a 75.1% stake in 2021, making it the UK's largest fan-owned club; around 8,000 fans still give about £1.7m a year.

name: Union Berlin
label: Fans bled for and rebuilt their club
why: In 2004 fans sold their blood and gave the money to the club to help secure its licence, and in 2008 thousands of volunteers put in an estimated 140,000 hours rebuilding the Alte Försterei. The club is still member-owned. Ownership is already 10, so this credits the rescue rather than the structure.

name: Shamrock Rovers
label: 400 Club fans saved the club
why: The 400 Club supporters' group took the club out of examinership in 2005 when it faced liquidation, and its successor, the Members Club, still owns 50% alongside Ray Wilson and Dermot Desmond.

name: Luton Town
label: Supporters' consortium rescue
why: Luton Town 2020, a consortium of local lifelong supporters, bought the club out of its third administration in 2008, took it from the -30-point season in League Two to the Premier League, and still runs it; it gave the Supporters' Trust shares, a board seat and a veto over identity changes. These are supporter-businessmen, not a mass-membership trust, hence medium.

name: Liverpool
label: Hillsborough justice and Hillsborough Law
why: The club has backed the families' decades-long justice campaign and publicly championed the Hillsborough Law (the Public Office (Accountability) Bill, with a duty of candour on officials), which became national legislation. The families led the campaign, and Values already notes it, so it sits at the low end of the range.

name: Eintracht Frankfurt
label: Stand against the far right (AfD)
why: President Peter Fischer said far-right AfD members were not welcome at the club, the club rejected AfD officials' membership applications, and he kept the stance until 2024. It drew national debate and legal complaints, and a prosecutor ruled it protected speech. Values credits the stance only lightly.

name: Bohemians
label: Refugee and humanitarian kit campaigns
why: The member-owned club ran a 'Refugees Welcome' kit with Amnesty in 2020, with all profits to asylum seekers in Direct Provision, and later kits raised money for Medical Aid for Palestinians and Palestine Sport for Life. Together they make a sustained, club-led cause identity. The sums are modest, so 2.

name: Arsenal
label: Pioneer of the English women's game
why: Arsenal founded its women's side in 1987, among the first English clubs to do so, turned it professional in 2002, and won the first British quadruple and the UEFA Women's Cup in 2007. It has kept investing since (2025 UWCL).

name: Lyon
label: Built the women's game's model club
why: From 2004 the club brought its women's team in-house and professionalised it well ahead of European peers, promising equal treatment. The team won a record eight Champions Leagues and set the template other clubs followed.

name: Kansas City Current
label: First stadium built for a women's pro team
why: The owners privately funded CPKC Stadium (about $117m, opened March 2024), the first stadium built for a women's professional team, plus a dedicated training centre, setting a facilities standard for the league.

name: Shakhtar Donetsk
label: Heart of Azovstal $25m pledge
why: After the Mudryk sale, owner Rinat Akhmetov and the club launched 'Heart of Azovstal', pledging $25m (UAH 1bn) for the medical, prosthetic and psychological care of Mariupol's defenders and their families. Reports disagree on whether the money came from the transfer fee itself.

name: Barcelona
label: Paid to carry UNICEF on the shirt
why: For its first ever shirt sponsor, the club gave the space to UNICEF and contributed €1.5m a year to joint projects, keeping the partnership to 2016. It gave up years of commercial shirt revenue, though a Qatar deal followed in 2011.

name: Rayo Vallecano
label: Housed an evicted 85-year-old neighbour
why: When 85-year-old Carmen Martínez Ayuso was evicted in Vallecas in 2014, coach Paco Jémez, his staff and players pledged to pay her rent, and the club opened a fund and gave gate money. It came at a modest cost but drew national attention.

name: Angel City FC
label: 10% sponsorship-to-community model
why: Since 2021 every partner has redirected 10% of its sponsorship value to local causes (reported at about $5.5m over three years), a model new to US pro sport. Values already credits the community model, so 1.
